mcqs.q: Besides restoring form and function, restorative therapy aims to:
opts: Minimize post-operative sensitivity and preserve pulp vitality
mcqs.explain: Restorative therapy should also minimize post-operative sensitivity and preserve pulp vitality.

mcqs.q: The MOST common irritant to the pulp is:
mcqs.explain: Caries is the most common pulpal irritant; others are the cavity-prep procedure, restorative materials and microleakage.

mcqs.q: An ideal pulp-protecting agent should be:
opts: Biocompatible, set quickly, low solubility and reduce dentin permeability
mcqs.explain: Ideal agents are biocompatible, set/harden quickly, have low solubility, withstand condensation forces and decrease dentin permeability.

mcqs.q: A cavity LINER is defined as a coating of minimal thickness, usually less than:
mcqs.explain: A cavity liner is a thin (<0.5 mm) cement/resin coating forming a barrier to bacteria or providing a therapeutic effect.

mcqs.q: The 'gold standard' liner for deep cavities is:
mcqs.explain: Calcium hydroxide (Hermann, 1930) is the long-standing gold-standard liner of choice in deep cavities.

mcqs.q: Calcium hydroxide protects the pulp because its hydroxyl ions:
opts: Create an alkaline pH that is antibacterial (and stimulate reparative dentin)
mcqs.explain: Hydroxyl ions create a high (alkaline) pH unfavourable to bacteria and stimulate reparative-dentin formation.

mcqs.q: Calcium hydroxide is specifically indicated for:
mcqs.explain: Calcium hydroxide is the material of choice for direct and indirect pulp capping.

mcqs.q: Cavity varnish is:
opts: A resin solution that evaporates to leave a thin film barrier
mcqs.explain: Cavity varnish is one or more resins in solvent; on application the solvent evaporates, leaving a thin resin film barrier.

mcqs.q: How many coats of cavity varnish should be applied?
mcqs.explain: Two coats are applied with a microapplicator, because a single application leaves voids.

mcqs.q: Cavity varnish is indicated:
opts: Below amalgam (to reduce microleakage) and below zinc phosphate
mcqs.explain: Varnish is used below amalgam (reducing initial microleakage) and below zinc phosphate cement.

mcqs.q: Cavity varnish is CONTRAINDICATED below composite because it:
mcqs.explain: The varnish film interferes with the bonding (and polymerization) of composite, so it is not used beneath composite restorations.

mcqs.q: Compared with a liner, a BASE is:
opts: A thicker layer providing thermal insulation and mechanical support
mcqs.explain: A base is a thicker layer that provides thermal insulation and mechanical support, replacing lost dentin.

mcqs.q: The composition of glass ionomer cement (GIC) is:
opts: Powder = fluoroaluminosilicate glass; liquid = polyacrylic acid
Powder = zinc oxide; liquid = phosphoric acid
mcqs.explain: GIC powder is fluoroaluminosilicate glass and the liquid is polyacrylic acid; it sets by an acid-base reaction.

mcqs.q: GIC sets by which type of reaction?
mcqs.explain: Conventional GIC sets by an acid-base reaction between the glass powder and the polyacid liquid.

mcqs.q: A major advantage of GIC is that it:
opts: Chemically bonds to tooth structure and releases fluoride
mcqs.explain: GIC chemically (ionically) bonds to tooth structure and releases fluoride (anticariogenic); it is also biocompatible.

mcqs.q: Which GIC TYPE is used for LUTING?
mcqs.explain: Type I GIC is for luting, Type II for restoration, Type III for liner/base.

mcqs.q: GIC TYPE II is used for:
mcqs.explain: Type II GIC is the restorative type, used for Class III and V restorations among others.

mcqs.q: GIC TYPE III is used as a:
mcqs.explain: Type III GIC is used as a liner or base.

mcqs.q: A disadvantage of conventional GIC is that it is:
opts: Brittle with relatively low strength (and moisture-sensitive early)
mcqs.explain: GIC is brittle with low strength and is moisture-sensitive during early setting, despite its bonding and fluoride benefits.

mcqs.q: Resin-modified glass ionomer (RMGI) differs from conventional GIC in that it:
opts: Adds resin and is light-cured, giving better strength while keeping fluoride/adhesion
mcqs.explain: RMGI combines glass ionomer with resin, allowing light-curing and improved strength while retaining fluoride release and adhesion.

mcqs.q: A glass-ionomer base may be placed over calcium hydroxide to:
opts: Prevent its dissolution and provide support
mcqs.explain: A GIC base over calcium hydroxide prevents dissolution of the (soluble) calcium hydroxide and adds support.

mcqs.q: Which protective material would you choose below COMPOSITE?
opts: A glass ionomer / RMGI liner (not varnish or eugenol)
mcqs.explain: Under composite, use GIC/RMGI (or calcium hydroxide); avoid varnish and eugenol-containing materials, which impair bonding/polymerization.

saqs.q: List the main pulpal irritants during restorative treatment.
saqs.a: Caries (commonest), the cavity-preparation procedure, restorative materials, and microleakage.

saqs.q: Define a cavity liner and name the traditional liners.
saqs.a: A thin (<0.5 mm) cement/resin coating forming a barrier/therapeutic layer. Traditional: calcium hydroxide, glass ionomer, RMGI.

saqs.q: Why is calcium hydroxide the liner of choice for deep cavities?
saqs.a: Its hydroxyl ions create an alkaline pH (antibacterial) and stimulate reparative dentin; used for pulp capping.

saqs.q: State the indications and contraindication of cavity varnish.
saqs.a: Indicated below amalgam (reduces microleakage) and zinc phosphate; contraindicated below composite (interferes with bonding).

saqs.q: Give the composition and setting reaction of GIC.
saqs.a: Powder = fluoroaluminosilicate glass; liquid = polyacrylic acid; sets by an acid-base reaction.

saqs.q: List two key advantages of GIC.
saqs.a: Chemically bonds to tooth and releases fluoride (anticariogenic); also biocompatible.

saqs.q: Give the three types of GIC and their uses.
saqs.a: Type I luting, Type II restorative, Type III liner/base.
